agent_notes: The Hebrew verse is the superscription, which the KJV leaves unnumbered (62:0 here, so every later KJV number is one lower). 'al yedutun is glossed 'on/according to Jeduthun'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as an instrument, Radak and Meiri as the Levite to whom the psalm was handed (Meiri reads 'al as 'el), and Rashi's midrash as 'on the decrees'. I kept the preposition literal and listed the readings in the commentary.

bene 'adam and bene 'ish are a merism of low and high (KJV 'low degree' and 'high degree', YLT 'the low' and 'the high'). The packet's gloss for 'adam and 'ish does not make the contrast, so I explained it in the commentary. 'in the balances to go up' is idiomatic: the last clause 'they are lighter than breath together' is Metzudat David's inverted reading, and I kept the Hebrew order literal.

hevel is the same root in v. 10 ('breath') and here as a verb tehbalu ('do not become breath', a denominative). The KJV 'become not vain' loses the echo with v. 10; The literal layer uses 'become breath' to keep the echo; the dramatic layer 'breathe yourselves thin' is looser. 'oshek and gazel are two different offenses (Radak: withholding what is owed vs forcible seizure; Ibn Ezra: by deceit vs by force).

The numerical proverb 'once ... twice' (x, x+1) is a standard Hebrew device (cf. Job 33:14, Prov 30:15); this citation is from my own knowledge and not from the packet. Rashi's two things (power and loving-kindness) come from the next verse (v. 13); Metzudat David and Malbim use the same pair. Radak instead reads 'once, twice' as 'many times'. I kept the literal sense and said the text itself names only 'strength belongs to God'.

agent_notes: Hapax-like verbs. tehotetu is read as from hawwot ('ruin, destruction') with Rashi's own view, Meiri and Metzudat Zion; Rashi also cites Menachem, who ties it to 'assemble' (cf. Jer 12:9), and a further view 'lengthen your tongues'. The Hebrew of 'terotzechu' is passive-voiced (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri on the Ben Asher reading with qamets) or active with patah (Ben Naphtali), so 'you will be murdered' (STEPBible) and 'you are all out to murder' are both defensible; I follow the passive qamets reading because the word is pointed that way in the packet. Rashi's 'ha-dechuyah' is a passive participle 'the thrust-down'. The KJV 'imagine mischief' and 'ye shall be slain' reflect the same split. The wall/fence image is syntactically open: Malbim's reading (a leaning wall that topples the shaky fence beneath it) is his own and I used it only as a possibility.

agent_notes: Corrected after review. lehadiach (from nadach, H5080) and hadechuyah (v. 4, from dachah, H1760) are different roots, so I say they echo in sound, as Ibn Ezra links the two ('and he mentioned lehadiach after the fence hadechuyah'). For mise'eto, Radak and Meiri read the suffix as God's loftiness; Metzudat David reads the plotters' own pride and loftiness as the motive. I follow the reading that the man under attack is the one who is being cast down from his height.
